project.name: Health Supply Chain Network Design
project.summary: A living map of a country's health supply chain that shows what it costs to reach every clinic — by road, boat and plane, month by month — and who gets left out when money is saved.

features.name: Usable by everyone
features.oneLiner: The whole screen works with a keyboard, reads correctly aloud, and holds up on a small display.

needsYou.title: The design work is finished and waiting on you
needsYou.text: All 23 accessibility checks and 288 automatic tests pass. It is saved on its own copy and has not joined the main project. Nothing is deployed anywhere yet.

stories.title: Use the whole tool with only a keyboard
stories.note: Six controls used to be mouse-only and silent to a screen reader.

stories.title: Read every label and figure clearly
stories.note: The faint grey most explanations were written in was too pale to read.

stories.title: Use it on a touch screen
stories.note: Buttons stay small for a mouse and grow to finger size only on a touch screen.

stories.title: Have it checked automatically so it cannot quietly break
stories.note: 23 checks, run with one command, and they fail loudly.

stories.title: Understand the screen without being shown it
stories.note: A fourteen-step guide dims the screen, lights up one control at a time and says what it is for. It opens by itself the first time and lives behind a Guide button after that.

stories.title: Use it comfortably on a phone
stories.unsure: It stacks and stays usable below 768 pixels, but has had no phone-first design pass.

decisions.what: The guide points at the live interface rather than showing screenshots, so it cannot drift out of date as the screen changes.
Buttons stay small for a mouse and grow to finger size only on a touch screen, so neither gets a compromise.
The accessibility check runs itself and fails loudly, so this cannot quietly rot later.

unsure: There is no light-colour version of the screen — it is dark only.

activity.what: A first-run guide now explains the map, the levers, the equity view and the seasons, pointing at the real controls
All 23 checks passed, on all nine panels, at six screen widths
Six controls that only worked with a mouse now work with a keyboard too

features.name: The map
features.oneLiner: Every clinic, store and delivery route in the country on one screen you can read at a glance.

stories.title: See every clinic, store and delivery route on one map
stories.note: 134 clinics, 5 stores and 39 timetabled services.

stories.title: Read the map with no internet connection at all
stories.unsure: The coastline we draw is rough — good to about 4km. Fine for showing where things are, not for measuring.

stories.title: Colour the map by how well each clinic is supplied
Switch on a detailed online map when there is a connection

decisions.what: The map must work with no internet at all. A provincial office often has none, so the coastline ships with the tool and online maps are an optional extra on top.
Decided against switching to Mapbox. It needs internet and a paid key, and would not change any answer the tool gives.

activity.what: Looked at using Mapbox instead and decided the current approach is better here
Ten real towns were being marked as out at sea — the coastline was wrong and is now fixed

features.name: Comparing plans side by side
features.oneLiner: Run several 'what if' plans at once and see cost, coverage and risk in one table.

stories.title: Compare several 'what if' plans side by side
stories.note: Today's network costs 11.24M kina a year and reaches everyone.

stories.title: Run every plan at once instead of waiting for each
See how each plan differs from how things work today
Download the comparison as a spreadsheet
File scenarios so a year of them stays findable
stories.note: Free-text tags on every scenario, chips that narrow the list as you add them, and a search box that also looks inside descriptions. A duplicate keeps its parent's tags.

stories.title: Name and revisit a particular version of a scenario
stories.unsure: Tags make scenarios findable; they do not freeze one. Saying 'this is what we showed the minister in March' still needs the input data versioned alongside the run, which it is not.

stories.title: Type a lever value instead of dragging to it
stories.note: Weights and switched-on constraints accept a typed number: 90%, 0.6, 2.5M.

stories.title: Start a study from a question and a preset
stories.note: Baseline vs cost-optimised, the equity floor pair, road/surface/air, wet season stress. Each is ordinary scenarios cloned from the baseline with one thing changed.

stories.title: Read what differs between the options and what it did
stories.note: A verdict paragraph, a lever diff per option, the facilities that gained or lost supply by name, the five bands side by side. Recommend marks the option the decision page carries.

stories.title: See two answers as one network on the map
stories.note: Lanes only the first uses red, only the second green, both grey; facilities that change supplier amber. Built from the stored flows, no solver work.

stories.title: A scenario can change the data, not only the levers, without touching the base
stories.note: Close a facility, scale demand, open a store, add or remove a lane. Applied in memory when it runs; listed in the lever diff; recorded in the ledger.

stories.title: Propose where new stores would go, from the demand itself
stories.note: Demand-weighted centre of gravity snapped to real facilities, with today's stores kept or dropped, drawn on the map; adopt it as a scenario of candidate stores the solver may open.

decisions.what: Tags are cleaned when they are stored, not when they are compared, so three spellings of one label cannot quietly split a filter.
Instead of forcing every plan to reach everyone, we put a price on not reaching someone. Every plan now gives an answer you can read, rather than some simply failing.

unsure: The costs, demand and boat timetables in the demo are illustrative, not the ministry's real figures. The clinic locations and the shape of the network are real.

activity.what: Greenfield site selection with adopt-as-scenario
Scenario items applied as an in-memory overlay; migration 0008
Studies: presets, ordered scenarios, verdict, lever diff, facilities moved, equity side by side, recommend, diff map; migration 0007
Scenarios can be tagged and filtered; filtering hides rows without changing what runs
Running seven plans at once was occasionally failing — found the cause and fixed it
Opening three new stores looked like it cost 4.5M a year more than it does — a one-off building cost was being counted as a yearly bill

features.name: Who pays for a saving
features.oneLiner: Shows which communities lose their supply when a plan saves money — before anyone decides.

stories.title: See which communities lose supply when a plan saves money
stories.note: Cutting cost by 19.5% moves 217,480 people from supplied to not supplied.

stories.title: See the number of people affected, not just a percentage
Set a floor that no community can fall below
stories.note: Holding the hardest-to-reach fifth at 90% still saves 9.3%.

decisions.what: Fairness is part of the sum, not a report at the end. A plan that saves money by giving up on the hardest-to-reach fifth has to say so in the same breath.

unsure: How we decide which communities are hardest to reach is our own definition. A ministry may well use a different one, and can change it.

activity.what: Checked the numbers hold up both ways round — the saving and the abandonment are the same figure seen from two sides

features.name: Month by month conditions
features.oneLiner: See what the wet season does — which roads close, and who can only be reached by plane.

stories.title: See which routes close in each month of the year
Re-price a whole plan for a single month
stories.note: In February 19 clinics cannot be reached at all and the plan costs 35.8% more.

stories.title: See who can only be reached by plane in the wet season
Solve a year as twelve linked months with stock carried between them
stories.note: Per-month flows under each month's access and cost, stock bounded by storage, a cyclic year. The Season tab shows the months and names the facilities that run short.

decisions.what: Every route carries twelve monthly access figures from the start, so the seasons are built in rather than bolted on later.

unsure: The seasonal patterns come from typical weather, not from records of roads actually closing. Worth checking with provincial staff before publishing anything.

activity.what: Multi-period solver, runner lever, four new KPIs, month table
February and July had no workable answer at all — changed the approach so every month gives a readable result naming who is affected

features.name: Getting your own data in
features.oneLiner: Download a spreadsheet, fill it in, upload it back. It is checked before anything is saved.

stories.title: Download a blank template to fill in
stories.note: Four sheets, 70 columns.

stories.title: See everything wrong with a file before any of it is saved
stories.note: 37 checks. Only six things are serious enough to stop an upload.

stories.title: Export everything back out again
stories.note: What you download and what you upload have identical columns.

stories.title: Start a new country without filling in 70 columns by hand
stories.unsure: Still nothing pre-fills a new country from open data. Only six fields are strictly required, but the workbook does not yet say which.

stories.title: Fix a flagged row without going back to the spreadsheet
stories.note: Correct it in the upload, it is re-checked immediately, and nothing is written until you apply.

stories.title: Import a CSV from another system by mapping its columns once
stories.note: Guesses the sheet and the headers, shows the mapping with the first row beside it, keeps the mapping per country under a name, and recognises it on the next file.

stories.title: A one-sheet file is merged, validated partially, never a wipe
stories.note: A facility list without lanes is not rejected; rows the file does not mention are left alone. Same preview and apply as a workbook.

decisions.what: Nothing is saved until you have seen the check results and said go ahead. A half-finished import is worse than one that stops, because nobody can tell which half is real.
What you download and what you upload have identical columns, so the work survives even if this tool does not.
Corrections happen inside the uncommitted upload, never against live data, so the two-step import stays the safety property it was.

unsure: Only Excel files are accepted. No CSV, and no older .xls.

activity.what: Column mapper for CSV imports: inspect, guess, map, save, validate partially, merge through the import pipeline
A clinic flagged 139 km out to sea can now be corrected in place and the block clears
Checked that exporting everything and importing it straight back changes nothing

features.name: Connecting to a country's own systems
features.oneLiner: Pull the clinic list and consumption straight out of the systems a ministry already runs.

stories.title: Pull the clinic list straight from DHIS2
stories.unsure: Only ever talked to a stand-in server we built, never a real ministry system.

stories.title: Pull from OpenLMIS
stories.unsure: Same — built and working, never tried against a real deployment.

stories.title: Pull from Open mSupply
stories.unsure: Papua New Guinea's own mSupply is an older version that does not offer this kind of connection.

stories.title: See every proposed change before anything is saved
stories.note: 6 clinics matched, 1 new, 1 moved, 1 renamed on the last run.

stories.title: Keep the delivery routes untouched when syncing
Keep passwords out of the tool entirely
stories.note: They can live outside it, so they never end up in a backup of it.

stories.title: Have a sync run on a schedule instead of by hand

decisions.what: A sync never touches the delivery routes. No stock system knows about boats, and losing the timetables would destroy the hardest part of the model to rebuild.

unsure: The whole feature needs one real ministry connection before anyone relies on it.

activity.what: A full pull, preview and save worked over a real network connection to a stand-in server
Two different clinics in the same town were being treated as one place because their names were trimmed too aggressively — fixed

features.name: The costed plan of action
features.oneLiner: Turns a chosen plan into a phased list of what to do, what it costs, and in what order.

stories.title: Turn a chosen plan into a phased list of what to do
See one-off costs separately from yearly running costs
Hand the plan to someone else as a document
stories.note: One self-contained HTML page that prints to PDF. Leads with the trade-off, names the people, states what it rests on.

stories.title: A decision page a minister can read on page one
stories.note: The recommendation, a map with the stores named, the stores table with capacity and facilities served, three numbers against today, the equity line, the confidence line. Every number links into the evidence.

stories.title: An assumptions annex written from the ledger
stories.note: How each value entered the model, counted; then the recent assumptions, corrections and estimates with who and why.

stories.title: A study report and a Decision view in the app
stories.note: The question over the backed option's decision page and the options considered. In the app, Decision hides levers and tabs and shows the options as cards.

decisions.what: One-off building costs are shown separately from yearly running costs, so a plan cannot look cheaper than it is.

unsure: How long each phase takes is an estimate, not drawn from how long this work actually takes in practice.

activity.what: Decision page on every report, study report, assumptions annex, Decision view toggle
A scenario can be handed over as a report rather than a spreadsheet
Checked the roadmap costs add up to the same total the plan reports

features.name: Selling this beyond one country
features.oneLiner: Turning a Papua New Guinea tool into something a consultant anywhere can pay to use.

stories.title: Set up a second country without a developer
stories.note: The coastline, terrain factors and seasonal profiles are country data now, not code.

stories.title: Sign in to your own account
stories.unsure: Nothing exists. Today anyone who reaches the tool can read and change everything in it.

stories.title: Pay for access
Hand a country over to a ministry when the work ends
stories.unsure: This is the promise the whole tool is sold on, and how the money would work is unresolved.

decisions.what: Wrote up what would have to be built and what the market looks like, including the parts that are uncomfortable.
A new country starts with a bounding box that rejects nothing. Inventing one would reject real facilities, which is worse than no check.

unsure: If the consultant is the one paying and the tool is meant to stay after they leave, who pays next year? Unresolved.
The consultants this would be sold to lost most of their funding in 2025. The need went up; the number of people with a budget went down.
The estimate of a few hundred people who would pay is our own guess, not a figure from anywhere.

activity.what: Opened a second country over the API with no code change, and its offshore check uses its own coastline
Wrote up what to build and what the market looks like, with the honest version of both

features.name: A record of every change
features.oneLiner: Who changed what, when, and how sure they were - kept as the model is edited, imported and re-run, and safe across upgrades.

stories.title: Upgrade the app without losing or deleting the database
stories.note: Schema changes are versioned migrations now. A database from before them is adopted at startup, not thrown away.

stories.title: See who made each change
stories.note: A name typed once per browser is written beside every change. Blank shows as "anonymous" on purpose.

stories.title: Read a lever change as one line, not forty slider notches
stories.note: Moves on the same lever in one sitting fold into a single row; sliding back to the start leaves none.

stories.title: Edit a facility's population, demand, volume or capacity in place
stories.note: Click a facility and edit its population, demand, capacity, coordinates and status in place. Every save declares sourced / inferred / unverified and is signed.

stories.title: Save a named session and reopen it exactly
stories.unsure: Planned after editing: dataset, ledger position, scenarios, results and report frozen together under a name.

stories.title: Upload a new master list without losing corrections made here
stories.note: An import shows what it would add, update, retire and restore before applying, and where the file disagrees with a correction it asks. Nothing is deleted.

stories.title: Add a facility by clicking the map, or retire one and bring it back
stories.note: Retiring keeps the history and takes the lanes and demand along; the Data tab lists retired facilities with Restore.

stories.title: Undo a hand-made change
stories.note: Revert from the Provenance tab. The original stays in the ledger marked reverted; the reversal names it.

stories.title: Fill a blank demand figure with a rule that shows its working
stories.note: From population, like peers, or storage from cover days. One row from the facility editor, or every blank row from the Data tab after a preview; each value is a ledger row with its arithmetic.

stories.title: Estimates follow their inputs until somebody types over them
stories.note: Change a population and the estimated demand moves, then the storage sized from it. Type a figure, or import one, and that row stops following.

stories.title: See how much of the model is estimated rather than recorded
stories.note: The overview and the Data tab say what share of demand rows is a rule's output. The seeded workspace says 100%, which is true.

stories.title: Know how much of an answer rests on estimates, and whether it survives them
stories.note: Every run re-solves with estimated demand 30% lower and higher. The scorecard says 'holds ±30%' or 'depends' per scenario; the report and spreadsheet carry the sentence and the range. A reversal is named, not averaged away.

stories.title: Edit any table in a grid, and set one field on many rows at once
stories.note: Facilities, lanes, products and demand. Lanes and products gained create, edit, retire and restore. A bulk edit is one ledger row per row in one batch.

decisions.what: The sensitivity runs inside every scenario run rather than on request. At ~50 ms a solve it is cheaper than a page load, and a check nobody has to ask for is the only one that is always there.

An estimate's rate is fixed when it is made and shown; only the row's own inputs are live. Re-learning the rate on every change would move every row whenever one facility's real data shifted the median.
Where a file disagrees with a correction made in the tool, the correction wins unless the person applying says otherwise, and the ledger records the choice either way.
Editing and saved sessions come before user accounts. Every change carries a typed author claim so accounts can inherit the history later by migration.
The column stopgap survives only to adopt old databases; every schema change from here is a migration.

unsure: A claim is a name, not a login: anyone can type any name until accounts exist.

activity.what: Table editor over every model table with filter, sort, inline edit, add, retire/restore and bulk set
Confidence budget: estimated share on every result, ±30% re-solves in the run, verdict in words on the scorecard, in the report and in the spreadsheet
Estimators: population rate, peer median and cover-days storage, live until pinned, every value a ledger row with its formula; the estimated share on the overview
Imports became a three-way diff with retire/restore instead of delete; in-place editing of facilities, demand and lane capacity with confidence markers; revert
Alembic migrations with automatic adoption of pre-migration databases; the audit trail became a ledger with author claims and batch ids

features.name: Saving and reopening your work
features.oneLiner: A session is the whole working state under a name: open it later and everything is exactly as saved, and the work it replaces is kept as a draft.

stories.title: Save the whole working state under a name
stories.note: Facilities, lanes, products, demand, scenarios, latest results and settings, with a note and the author's name. Two saves of the same state share one snapshot.

stories.title: Open a session and get back exactly what was saved
stories.note: Ids included, so saved results still point at their facilities. Whatever you were doing is kept as a draft first; naming a draft makes it a save.

stories.title: Read what differs between two sessions in sentences
stories.note: Compare a session with the screen or with another session: facilities moved, demand estimated, scenarios re-levered, costs changed.

stories.title: See how much has changed since the session you are working from
stories.note: Counted in sittings, not ledger rows, so one population edit that moved eight estimates reads as one change.

stories.title: Studies: a question, its scenarios, its verdict, and the diff map
stories.note: Built under 'Comparing plans side by side'.

decisions.what: A session snapshot is the model itself, every column of every row, not a file pushed back through the import pipeline. An import must be validated and reconciled; a restore must be exact, and serialising columns generically is what keeps the two from drifting.
The saved session is immutable. Opening it copies it into the working state; the working state is drafted first so no edit can be lost by looking at an older save.

unsure: Snapshots live in the database as gzipped blobs (about 100 KB each for PNG). Fine for hundreds; a country with ten thousand facilities and daily saves will want them on object storage.

activity.what: Sessions shelf: save, open with automatic draft, compare in words, rename and delete; migration 0006; the demo carries an empty shelf

parkingLot.name: Mapbox as the map
parkingLot.note: Looked at properly and set aside. It needs an internet connection and a paid key, and roads carry only 11.5% of the cost in this model — so it would not change any answer. The reasoning is written down.

parkingLot.name: Better-looking offline map
parkingLot.note: A sharper map that still needs no internet. The genuinely useful version of the Mapbox idea we turned down. Nothing started.

parkingLot.name: Real road distances
parkingLot.note: The tool already has a place for this to plug into. Until it does, road distances are informed estimates and the tool says so on every one.

parkingLot.name: Collecting data on phones in the field
parkingLot.note: For countries where the information does not exist yet and has to be gathered. Would use the survey tools the sector already uses rather than a new app.

parkingLot.name: Accounts, logins and payment
parkingLot.note: Needed before anyone could pay for access. Planned out in detail, not begun — it is the first thing to build if the answer is yes.
